title: The Average Stock Shrugged Off the Tech Slide. History Is Split
detail:
The Average Stock Shrugged Off the Tech Slide. History Is Split
Trefis Team
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 4:18 PM CST 6 min read

SPX
RSP
QQQ
IWM
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

For most of this bull market, investors could count on one rule. The biggest stocks lead. When a few tech giants rise, the S&P 500 rises with them. When they fall, the rest of the market falls too. Over the past month, that rule bent. From Oct. 23 to Nov. 24, the regular S&P 500 fund (SPY) lost 5.42%. The equal-weight S&P 500 fund (RSP), which gives each of the 500 companies the same weight, lost only 1.19%. The Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) fund lost 9.41% over the same dates. The average stock fell far less than the giants, after the giants' lead hit a record on Oct. 7. Whether that lasts is the open question.

The Nasdaq-100 fund fell 9.41% in a single month while the average stock lost only 1.19%. A drop like that is easier to sit through when your savings do not hang on a few tech stocks. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

How the Biggest Stocks Took Over

One simple gauge tracks this rule. Take the value of the equal-weight fund, with dividends reinvested, and divide it by the value of the regular S&P 500 fund on the same day. The ratio falls when the biggest stocks do better than the average one. At the end of 2014 it stood at 0.388. That was its highest year-end reading in data that start in 2003.

Then it slid for a decade. The ratio was 0.328 at the end of 2023, 0.296 at the end of 2024 and 0.280 at the end of 2025. It kept falling this year. On Oct. 7 it reached 0.271, the lowest since the data begin.

What Changed This Year

The ratio turned in early October. From its Oct. 7 low of 0.271, it climbed to 0.298 on Nov. 24. That is above its reading of 0.280 at the end of 2025.

Over the year as a whole, the average stock has also beaten tech. From Dec. 31, 2025 to Nov. 24, the equal-weight fund returned 13.03%, dividends included. The Nasdaq-100 fund returned 4.23%. But the largest S&P 500 names kept their lead over the average stock until early October.

Correlation measures how closely two prices move together, where 1 means in lockstep and 0 means unrelated. The equal-weight fund and the Nasdaq-100 fund have moved less closely day to day this year. Their correlation of daily moves has averaged 0.57 so far in 2026, tied with 2021 for the lowest yearly average in data back to 2015. In 2022 it averaged 0.89. Over the last 63 trading days it was 0.66 as of Nov. 24. So lately the two funds have moved a bit more in step day to day. Over the past month they still moved by very different amounts.

title: 2 Bargain Stocks to Buy With $1,000 in November
detail:
2 Bargain Stocks to Buy With $1,000 in November
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 4:47 PM CST 4 min read

^GSPC

Trading disclosure

Novo Nordisk's (NYSE:NVO) yield is historically high at 4.4%. The same is true of PepsiCo's (NASDAQ:PEP) 4.1% yield. By comparison, the S&P 500 index's (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) yield is a mere 1%. That suggests both are bargains as November draws to a close. Here's a closer look at why you should consider putting $1,000 into each one of these bargain stocks.

Novo Nordisk: The guidance is heading higher

Novo Nordisk is a pharmaceutical company that is leaning into its Wegovy/Ozempic GLP-1 weight-loss portfolio. Wall Street is worried for two main reasons. First, it fumbled the ball after being the first to market with this new class of drugs. Second, it is shifting its business model to one driven by volume, which has required it to lower prices.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

As to the first concern, Novo Nordisk's execution of its GLP-1 shot wasn't great, as it struggled to keep up with demand. It has been much better with its recent pill launch, which has seen dramatically higher demand. Moreover, there's likely room for more than one weight-loss drug given the size of the addressable market, so falling into second place in the GLP-1 space isnt the end of the world. Meanwhile, lowering prices has, indeed, hurt revenues and earnings. But the company upped its full-year 2026 guidance when it reported third-quarter 2026 earnings. That suggests that the volume-led transition is going well.

Novo Nordisk's 4.4% yield is historically high and well above the pharmaceutical industry average of 1.3%. Its roughly 10x price-to-earnings ratio is also well below the industry average of 27x. It looks like a bargain for more aggressive income investors, and a $1,000 investment will net you roughly 24 shares.

PepsiCo: Making the right moves and muddling through

PepsiCo is one of the world's largest consumer staples companies. It is an industry leader in the snack and beverage areas, and it has a sizable packaged food business as well. It is more diversified than most of its peers, and it can stand toe-to-toe with any of them as a business, with strong brands, marketing, innovation, and distribution.

The problem is that PepsiCo's business isn't firing on all cylinders right now, with its organic sales growth notably lagging that of key peer Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO). Still, PepsiCo's 3.1% organic sales growth in the third quarter wasn't bad, even though it was less than half of Coca-Cola's 7%. But investors remain worried, thanks notably to weakness in PepsiCo's large U.S. operations.

Matias Civita

Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

U.S. stocks staged a partial recovery Wednesday after a dramatic morning sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence investments, accelerating inflation, and President Donald Trump's plans to impose additional tariffs on major trading partners.

The Nasdaq Composite, which plunged as much as 4.6% earlier in the session, was down 0.8% as of 3:07 p.m. ET. The S&P 500 narrowed its losses to 0.3% after falling as much as 3.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average reversed its earlier decline to gain 244 points, or 0.5%.

The volatile session came ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, with investors confronting growing uncertainty about the technology sector and the direction of Federal Reserve monetary policy.

Nvidia was among the companies driving the technology sell-off, with shares tumbling approximately 8% during morning trading as concerns mounted over the profitability of artificial intelligence investments.

The decline followed a short-lived relief rally Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive. His return initially helped restore confidence in the semiconductor sector, but enthusiasm quickly faded.

Investors have increasingly questioned whether the billions of dollars companies are committing to AI infrastructure, data centers and advanced computing equipment will generate enough revenue to justify elevated valuations.

Anthropic has also faced selling pressure following its highly anticipated initial public offering last week. Shares of the artificial intelligence company fell below their IPO price Tuesday. The technology sector's struggles have weighed heavily on the broader market. The S&P 500 has lost approximately 5.5% in November, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 have been on track for their worst November performances since 2008.

Additional pressure came from Wednesday's inflation report, which showed that the core Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, climbed 3.3% annually in October, exceeding economists' expectations of 3.2%.

The reading reinforced expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates at its December meeting. Traders priced in a 98% probability of a quarter-percentage-point increase following the report.

Higher interest rates present a particular challenge for technology companies because they increase borrowing costs and reduce the present value of projected future earnings. Meanwhile, separate data showed the U.S. economy grew considerably faster than previously estimated during the third quarter.
